# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke, accounting for a substantial proportion of cardioembolic events [1]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC), with either vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention in patients with AF [2]. However, a significant proportion of patients have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation or experience bleeding complications [3]. Because the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the source of more than 90% of thrombi in non-valvular AF, mechanical exclusion of the LAA has emerged as an attractive alternative for stroke prophylaxis [4]. Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has therefore developed rapidly over the past two decades [5].

## Rationale and Anatomy

The LAA is a trabeculated, embryologically distinct structure with highly variable morphology, commonly classified as "chicken wing," "windsock," "cactus," and "cauliflower" types [6]. This anatomical heterogeneity has direct implications for device selection and procedural success [7]. Stasis of blood within the appendage during AF promotes thrombus formation, providing the pathophysiological basis for LAAC [4]. Preprocedural imaging with transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and increasingly cardiac computed tomography is essential for accurate sizing and exclusion of pre-existing thrombus [8].

## Devices and Procedure

Two endocardial device families dominate contemporary practice. The Watchman device (and its successor Watchman FLX) is a self-expanding nitinol cage deployed across the LAA ostium [9]. The Amplatzer Amulet uses a distinct lobe-and-disc design intended to seal the ostium more proximally [10]. Both are deployed via transseptal catheterization under fluoroscopic and echocardiographic guidance [11]. Epicardial approaches, such as the LARIAT suture ligation system, offer an alternative that avoids leaving an endocardial implant, though evidence remains more limited [12].

## Clinical Evidence

The pivotal PROTECT AF trial demonstrated that Watchman closure was non-inferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death in patients with non-valvular AF [13]. The subsequent PREVAIL trial addressed early procedural safety concerns and confirmed acceptable outcomes [14]. Long-term follow-up of these trials, pooled in a patient-level meta-analysis, showed reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular mortality compared with warfarin [15,16]. Registry data, including the EWOLUTION study, confirmed favorable real-world safety and efficacy [17]. The PRAGUE-17 randomized trial extended the comparison to DOACs, showing non-inferiority of LAAC to DOAC therapy in high-risk patients [18,19].

The Amulet IDE trial randomized patients to the Amulet versus Watchman device and demonstrated non-inferiority for safety and effectiveness, with the Amulet achieving higher rates of complete closure [20]. Comparative meta-analyses have generally shown similar efficacy across devices [21].

## Procedural Safety and Complications

Major complications include pericardial effusion and tamponade, device embolization, procedure-related stroke, and vascular access complications [22]. Operator experience and procedural volume strongly influence complication rates, which have declined as techniques and devices have matured [23]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in approximately 3–4% of patients and is associated with an increased risk of thromboembolic events [24]. Peri-device leak, identified on follow-up imaging, is another concern whose clinical significance remains under investigation [25].

## Antithrombotic Management and Surveillance

The optimal post-procedural antithrombotic regimen remains debated. Initial protocols used short-term warfarin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy and then aspirin monotherapy [13]. Many contemporary practices use DOAC-based or dual antiplatelet strategies, particularly in patients with bleeding contraindications [26]. Imaging surveillance, typically at 45 days and several months post-implant, assesses device position, residual leak, and DRT [8]. The duration and intensity of antithrombotic therapy must be individualized to balance thromboembolic and bleeding risks [27].

## Guidelines and Future Directions

Current guidelines assign LAAC a role primarily in patients with contraindications to long-term anticoagulation, reflecting the limitations of available randomized data [2,28]. Ongoing large randomized trials such as CHAMPION-AF and OPTION are evaluating LAAC against DOACs in broader populations, which may expand indications [29]. Combined procedures—such as concomitant LAAC and catheter ablation—are also being explored [30]. Refinements in device design, improved imaging, and standardized antithrombotic protocols are expected to further enhance outcomes.

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC has become an established alternative for stroke prevention in selected patients with non-valvular AF, particularly those unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation. Robust randomized data support its non-inferiority to warfarin, and emerging evidence suggests comparability to DOACs. Continued attention to procedural safety, device-related thrombus, and individualized antithrombotic management will be central to optimizing patient outcomes as indications potentially broaden.
